payload.description: Add a user-only command that appends a correcting ledger event setting a task's status directly, with a required reason, so a wrong state is fixed without replaying lifecycle transitions that never happened.
payload.context: The ledger is append-only, and the only way to correct a task's state today is to replay ordinary transitions through their gates. payload.title: Decide moving Endless's records off the default branch
payload.description: Decide moving the records Endless commits by itself (ledger entries, task-field and decision mirrors, lessons, verify reports) from a project's default branch to a separate branch, linked to main by a commit trailer
payload.plan:
## Open questions

**Q1. What is the trailer's key?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Fixed: `endless-main: <sha>` | One key to search for in every repo. | Reads wrong in a repo whose default branch is not main. |
| B. Named for the default branch: `endless-<primary_branch>: <sha>` | Says which branch the SHA is on. | The key differs per repo, so a reader must know the branch name to search; renaming the branch changes the key for new commits only. |
| C. Fixed key, branch in the value: `endless-base: main@<sha>` (or two trailers, `endless-branch` and `endless-commit`) | One key everywhere, and it still names the branch. | none |

Recommendation: C.

**Q2. What is the branch called?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. `endless-meta` | Matches the separate-repo naming convention. | none |
| B. `endless/meta` (a namespace) | Leaves room for other Endless branches under `endless/`. | A branch named `endless` can then never exist, since git cannot hold both. |

Recommendation: A.

**Q3. How does Endless write to the branch while main is checked out?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Git's low-level commands (`hash-object`, `mktree`, `commit-tree`, `update-ref`) with no checkout | No extra directory; no working tree to get dirty. | Reading a record means `git show` against the branch instead of opening a file. |
| B. A dedicated worktree of the branch (e.g. under `.endless/worktrees/`) | Records stay ordinary files that tools and people can open. | One more working tree that can be left dirty or deleted by hand. |

Recommendation: A for writes, with reads going through Endless's commands.

**Q4. When does a clone fetch the branch?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Before every read of records | Always current. | A network call on each read; offline reads need a fallback to the local copy. |
| B. On a schedule, alongside main-sync's fetch | Reads stay local and fast. | Records can be minutes stale. |

Recommendation: B, with A available as an explicit refresh.

**Q5. What happens to records already on main?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Copy them to the new branch, then delete them from main's tree in one commit | Main's tree is clean from then on; history keeps the old copies. | One large deletion commit on main. |
| B. Leave existing records on main; only new records go to the branch | No large commit. | Records split across two places forever. |

Recommendation: A.

Endless commits to a project's default branch far more often than at lands: ledger entries, task-field and decision mirrors, lessons and verify reports, each as its own commit. They clutter main's history, and GitHub names a push-triggered CI run after the push's newest commit, so runs get titled "Endless: record ledger entry" or "lesson: ..." (seen on go-dt). Settled with Mike, 2026-10-29 (in E-2375's session):

payload.title: Refuse to verify a task that has already landed
payload.description: Refuse `endless task verify` on an already-landed task with a message saying it landed (and where), instead of the reconciliation gate's false 'the code changed' error
payload.context:
Running `endless task verify E-2419` after E-2419 landed (status `assumed`, branch HEAD a1cfd49 on main) refused with:

    Error: E-2419 cannot be verified yet:
      - the code changed since the last reconciliation; reconcile again

The message is false. The reconciliation gate (internal/reconcilegate, `Fingerprint`) fingerprints the branch as the patch-id of its diff from the merge-base with main to HEAD. Once the branch is in main, the merge-base is HEAD, the diff is empty, and the fingerprint is "empty" — which never matches the one stored at reconciliation. So every landed task gets this error, and reconciling again cannot clear it.

Verifying a landed task should not run at all: a suite is a land-time gate (.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md), and a pass would call `unlanded.record_pass` (src/endless/verify_cmd.py), moving the task's state on a run that means nothing.

# Update an unedited .endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md on project init

Handed over from E-2349 (Mike asked its session to send it). Filed from E-2257
on Mike's go-ahead, 2026-10-22.

## Problem

Every project Endless manages gets a rules file at `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.
It tells an agent how a task's own folder works and how to write a verify
suite. Endless writes it the first time `endless project init` runs, and never
touches it again.

Re-running `endless project init` is meant to bring a project up to date
(E-2349's EQ-82). For this file it doesn't. So when Endless changes the rules,
as E-2419 did, every existing project keeps the old ones: go-cfgstore and
homelab still teach the old suite form today.

## Behaviour

Re-running init updates the file to the rules this Endless ships, but only if
nobody has edited the project's copy:

- If the file is exactly what init last wrote into this project, replace it.
- If init has no record for this project (the copy predates this feature), and
  the file is exactly some version Endless has shipped, replace it.
- Otherwise leave it alone, and say it was edited locally and not updated.

"Exactly" is judged by a hash of the file's contents, so Endless never has to
keep the old text itself.

## Where the records live

- **What init wrote into a project** belongs to that project, so it is
  recorded in the project's own history (the ledger) and travels with a clone.
- **Which versions Endless has shipped** belongs to Endless itself, so each
  install knows them with no download or setup.
- If both are kept in one place, it can hold other kinds of shipped file later,
  not just this one (Mike).
- Hashing and storage are done in Go; everything is moving there (Mike).

## Content

- A list of what changed may go in the file itself, as text a reader sees
  (Mike).

## In the endless repo itself

- Running init from a task's worktree records into that worktree's sandbox,
  not the main database.

## Blocked by

- E-2419, which changed the rules text. It has landed.

## Open questions

**Q1. What is the trailer's key?** The value names Git's default branch and the commit, e.g. `main@<sha>`. A trailer key must be letters, digits and hyphens: `git interpret-trailers --parse` ignores a line whose key has other characters.

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. `endless-default: main@<sha>` | Names Endless. | Reads as a default of Endless's, which it is not. |
| B. `git-default: main@<sha>` | Uses Git's own term. | Does not say Endless wrote it, so it could collide with another tool's trailer. |
| C. `Endless[git-default]: main@<sha>` | Names Endless and gives a pattern for later annotations. | Git does not recognize it as a trailer, so `git interpret-trailers` and `git log --format=%(trailers)` never see it. |
| D. `endless-git-default: main@<sha>` | Names Endless and uses Git's term; the `endless-<name>` prefix is a pattern for later annotations, and git recognizes it. | none |
| E. `endless-base: main@<sha>` | Names Endless; short. | "base" is not Git's term for the default branch. |
| F. `endless_git-default: main@<sha>` | Names Endless; underscore separates the namespace. | Git does not recognize it: an underscore is not allowed in a trailer key. |
| G. `endless:git-default: main@<sha>` | Names Endless; colon reads as a namespace. | Git splits at the first colon, so it parses as key `endless` with value `git-default: main@<sha>`. |

Recommendation: D. (Options A to C, F and G were Mike's, 2026-10-29; F and G tested with git interpret-trailers --parse.)

**Q2. What is the branch called?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. `endless-meta` | Matches the separate-repo naming convention. | none |
| B. `endless/meta` (a namespace) | Leaves room for other Endless branches under `endless/`. | A branch named `endless` can then never exist, since git cannot hold both. |

Recommendation: A.

**Q3. How does Endless write to the branch while main is checked out?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Git's low-level commands (`hash-object`, `mktree`, `commit-tree`, `update-ref`) with no checkout | No extra directory; no working tree to get dirty. | Reading a record means `git show` against the branch instead of opening a file. |
| B. A dedicated worktree of the branch (e.g. under `.endless/worktrees/`) | Records stay ordinary files that tools and people can open. | One more working tree that can be left dirty or deleted by hand. |

Recommendation: A for writes, with reads going through Endless's commands.

**Q4. When does a clone fetch the branch?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Before every read of records | Always current. | A network call on each read; offline reads need a fallback to the local copy. |
| B. On a schedule, alongside main-sync's fetch | Reads stay local and fast. | Records can be minutes stale. |

Recommendation: B, with A available as an explicit refresh.

**Q5. What happens to records already on main?**

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. Copy them to the new branch, then delete them from main's tree in one commit | Main's tree is clean from then on; history keeps the old copies. | One large deletion commit on main. |
| B. Leave existing records on main; only new records go to the branch | No large commit. | Records split across two places forever. |

Recommendation: A.

## Approach

**The Git hook.** A `prepare-commit-msg` script that reads the branch with `git symbolic-ref --short -q HEAD`, matches `task/<N>`, and, when the message file has no `Endless-Task` trailer, appends one with `git interpret-trailers --in-place --if-exists doNothing --trailer "Endless-Task: E-<N>"`. fields.plan:
# Require plan approval before a task reports its work

Approval of a task's plan items has to happen before the task is handed in as
done. Once a task is `unverified`, its items can no longer change, approval
included, so an approval skipped before that point can't be given afterwards.
Requiring it at the hand-in closes that path.

## Approach

The check goes in the reconciliation gate (`internal/reconcilegate`, `check`),

payload.plan:
# Name the event in each ledger commit's subject

## Problem

Every ledger auto-commit is titled `Endless: record ledger entry`. `git log` on
any project Endless manages is a wall of identical subjects, and nothing in one
says which event it holds.

## Change

Title each ledger commit by its event: the kind and the entity, within 60
characters, e.g. `Endless: task.status_changed E-2421`, or
`Endless: shipped_file.written .endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`, shortened to fit.

## The coupling that makes this more than a string change

The subject is the key the amend logic matches on:

- Go `events.LedgerCommitSubject` — `canAmend` amends only when HEAD's subject
  equals the subject being committed, so successive ledger commits fold into one.
- Python `worktree_cmd.AMENDABLE_COMMIT_SUBJECTS`, and anything else that
  recognises a ledger commit by its exact subject.

With unique subjects, exact-match amending stops folding ledger commits

# Update an unedited .endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md on project init

Handed over from E-2349 (Mike asked its session to send it). Filed from E-2257
on Mike's go-ahead, 2026-10-22.

## Problem

Every project Endless manages gets a rules file at `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.
It tells an agent how a task's own folder works and how to write a verify
suite. Endless writes it the first time `endless project init` runs, and never
touches it again.

Re-running `endless project init` is meant to bring a project up to date
(E-2349's EQ-82). For this file it doesn't. So when Endless changes the rules,
as E-2419 did, every existing project keeps the old ones: go-cfgstore and
homelab still teach the old suite form today.

## Behaviour

Re-running init updates the file to the rules this Endless ships, but only if
nobody has edited the project's copy:

- If the file is exactly what init last wrote into this project, replace it.
- If init has no record for this project (the copy predates this feature), and
  the file is exactly some version Endless has shipped, replace it.
- Otherwise leave it alone, and say it was edited locally and not updated.

"Exactly" is judged by a hash of the file's contents, so Endless never has to
keep the old text itself.

## Where the records live

- **What init wrote into a project** belongs to that project, so it is
  recorded in the project's own history (the ledger) and travels with a clone.
- **Which versions Endless has shipped** belongs to Endless itself, so each
  install knows them with no download or setup.
- If both are kept in one place, it can hold other kinds of shipped file later,
  not just this one (Mike).
- Hashing and storage are done in Go; everything is moving there (Mike).

## Content

- A list of what changed may go in the file itself, as text a reader sees
  (Mike).

## In the endless repo itself

- Running init from a task's worktree records into that worktree's sandbox,
  not the main database.

## After the first land: the default branch and every worktree

Added after E-2421 first landed, while still live in the session that landed
it (ED-1550), on Mike's direction:

- **Off the default branch, init does nothing.** Whatever it writes there would
  sit uncommitted until that branch merged, if it ever did. The off-branch
  behaviour before this was an omission: E-2349 decided only that nothing is
  committed there. Init refuses and says to switch to the default branch.
- **On the default branch** the update is committed together with the rest of
  the bring-up, and its record goes into the project's ledger.
- **Every worktree of the project gets the update now**, not when its task
  lands. Each copy is judged on its own, without the record (which describes
  the default branch): an unedited copy is written and committed on that
  worktree's branch. A copy edited there is left alone and named. Committed,
  not just written, because `endless worktree land` refuses a worktree with
  uncommitted files (E-1416). A fresh commit rather than a cherry-pick: a
  worktree that branched at an older version would make the cherry-pick
  conflict. At land the rebase drops the commit, since the default branch
  already has the same file.
- **The record follows the file.** A copy already current whose record says
  otherwise is recorded again; otherwise the next shipped version would read
  it as an edit.

## Blocked by

- E-2419, which changed the rules text. It has landed.

# Research request: how every Endless session learns to leave other projects' work to those projects

## Why

A session in one project read its own plan step ("check each dependency for uncommitted work, commit, push") as authority over another project's in-flight work, and proposed committing and tagging it. Mike corrected it: work in a project is managed by a task in that project, run by a session for that project. Neither the guide nor any CLAUDE.md says so, and a plan can appear to say the opposite. The rule must be unmissable and must hold even against a plan that seems to grant the authority.

## Questions to answer

1. Does a task or decision already cover this? Search tasks and decisions for cross-project work, delegation, dependency, uncommitted work, release and ownership. Read the decision on searching for an owning task before filing. If one exists, the finding goes there as evidence and nothing new is filed.
2. Where does a session learn its rules today, and which of those places should carry this one? # Resolve a named session or task in any project

## Change

Two parts, one cause: a session's project decides where it can be found, and
that project is wrong for any session working another project's task.

### 1. Lookups by id ignore the cwd's project

- `endless-go session-query list-live` gains `--all-projects`, which drops the
  `s.project_id` filter in `monitor.ListLiveSessions`. `--project-root` keeps
  its meaning for listings.
- `session_cmd._live_sessions` takes an all-projects mode. Every caller that
  resolves one named session or task uses it: `session goto`, `show`, `cd`,
  `use`, `back`, `_resume_in_background`, `show_history`, and
  `_live_window_claiming` (the `--rebind` guard). So does finding the current
  window's session when no id is given (`_resolve_companion`), since a pane
  is as specific as an id.
- Each row's `worktree_path` is computed from the session's own project path,
  not the cwd's. `list-live` rows carry the project's path for this.
- `goto` and the background resume act in the session's own project and
  worktree.

### 2. A session's project is its task's project

- `bindSessionTask` (task.claimed, task.bound) also sets `sessions.project_id`
  to the claimed task's `project_id`.
- `monitor.BindSessionToTask` (the hook's auto-bind from a worktree) takes the
  project from the task, not from its caller.
- A session with no task keeps the project it was created with. Releasing a
  task leaves the session's project unchanged.
- A schema migration re-stamps every existing session that has a `task_id`
  with that task's project. Session rows are written directly, not rebuilt
  from the ledger, so nothing else would fix them.
- The project a session started in is not stored anywhere new: session_tasks
  already records which tasks it touched.

## Verify

- From go-cfgstore, `session goto`, `show`, `cd` on a live session recorded
  under another project find it.
- Claiming a go-cfgstore task from a session started in endless leaves
  `sessions.project_id` at go-cfgstore, and the next hook event does not move
  it back.
- `session list` in a project still shows only that project's sessions, now
  including sessions working its tasks.

# Refuse to resume a Claude session that is already running

Builds on E-2358, which makes session lookups by id search every project
(`list-live --all-projects`).

## Change

### One check before every resume launch

A function in `session_cmd` (e.g. `_refuse_if_running`) runs immediately
before each `claude --resume <uuid>` launch: `session resume` (exec in the
current pane), `session goto --resume` (new window, `_resume_new_window_pane`)
and `goto --resume --background` (`_resume_in_background`). It refuses when
either holds:

1. The target's Claude session UUID belongs to a session that reads `live`
   among live sessions in every project.
2. A running `claude` process has `--resume <the target's UUID>` in its
   arguments (a process listing). This catches a resume started by hand,
   which liveness does not track.

`--new-transcript` opens a new transcript, so it is not checked.

### What each command says

- `session resume` and `goto --resume --background` refuse: the session is
  already running; run `endless session goto <ref>`.
- `session goto --resume` on a running target fails rather than quietly
  focusing it: the session is already running; drop `--resume`, i.e. run
  `endless session goto <ref>`.
- A target that reads `unknown` or `unbound` stays resumable unless the
  process check finds it.

### Sessions on servers that predate socket recording read dead

`session_liveness` reads `unknown` for a session whose tmux server was not
reached and is not proven gone. Endless now records a server's socket on the
first hook on it (`recordTmuxServer`), but servers that died before that
recording existed have none, so their sessions read `unknown` forever.
Liveness already scans every directory tmux puts sockets in
(`observeTmuxServers`: the default socket directory and Endless's). Add the
rule: a session whose server has no row in `tmux_servers` and was not seen
in that scan reads `dead`. No session rows are written; every machine's old
rows read correctly.

## Verify

- Resuming a session live in another project refuses and names
  `endless session goto <ref>`.
- `goto --resume` on a live session fails and says to drop `--resume`.
- With a `claude --resume <uuid>` process running outside any pane Endless
  knows, resuming that uuid refuses.
- Sessions on unrecorded, unobserved servers read `dead`; `list-live` no
  longer lists them.

payload.title: Design how sessions hand over paste-safe commands
payload.description: Design how a session hands the user commands that paste without editing: no wrapping in Claude's tmux pane, ~ for home, no long tmp paths, and where that rule lives so it sticks across sessions.
payload.context:
Raised while handing off E-2376 in go-logutil, where the user had to edit the
commands the session handed them, and said they have asked for this before
without it sticking.

## The two problems

1. **Commands wrap and break on paste.** A long single-line command in a
   fenced block wraps in the tmux pane where the Claude session runs. Copying
   the wrapped text picks up newlines and spaces at the wrap points, so the
   pasted command fails. The session cannot see the pane width, so it has no
   signal that a line will wrap.

2. **Paths are longer than they need to be.** Sessions write the home
   directory out in full instead of `~`, and hand over scratchpad or tmp
   filenames so long they wrap twice. Beyond the paste problem, a long path
   makes the command hard to scan for what it does.

## Why instructions so far have not stuck

- Nothing the session reads says it. The guide's one-command handoff
  contract, the handoff template and the project CLAUDE.md files say WHICH
  command to hand over, not its shape.
- The Claude Code harness tells a session to write scratchpad paths
  "complete and absolute, in one piece", a nudge against half of the rule.
- Lessons do not reach a session. The go-pkgs CLAUDE.md forbids reading
  LESSONS.md, so a lesson written there (go-logutil has one on this, written
  2026-10-31) cannot change the next session's behavior unless Endless folds
  it into something the session does read.
- It is a formatting habit; compliance decays over a long session even with
  the rule in context.

## Related finding from the same conversation

The session was asked whether a hook could reliably extract the commands a
session hands over from its prose. Its answer: not reliably. Fences are
untagged or inconsistently tagged; fences also hold error text, file content
and TOML; inline code spans sometimes carry commands, sometimes with
placeholders; and which fence is "the" verify command lives only in the
prose. A structured channel (a command or tool call with typed fields) is
the only parse-free route; a tagging convention enforced by a Stop hook is
the next best.

## Candidate resolutions to weigh

- A rule in the user's global CLAUDE.md (covers every project, every
  session) naming a column budget, `~` for home, a `cd` line before long
  relative paths, and no scratchpad paths.
- A sentence in the guide's one-command handoff contract and in the
  handoff templates, so it lands at the point of use.
- A Stop hook that rejects a reply whose fenced block has a line over the
  budget or contains the absolute home path.
- A structured channel for handed-over commands (`endless task report` or
  similar), which also answers the extraction question.
- Feeding relevant lessons back into the handoff a spawned session reads.
- Having Endless tell the session the pane width (tmux knows it), so the
  budget is a fact, not a guess.
payload.justification: The user wants to work out the resolution themselves in the Endless project, not in the go-logutil session where it surfaced; the options span CLAUDE.md, the guide, the handoff template, hooks and a structured report channel, and choosing among them is a design decision.

# Plan

Answer the five questions in this task's context with counts from real
transcripts and the hook log, then report measured capture and
false-positive rates for a candidate hook rule.

## Sample

Endless-driven sessions from the last month. Find them through Endless's
session records (harness session ids on ES- sessions created in the last
30 days) and map each to its transcript JSONL under the Claude projects
directory in the user's home. Sessions with no transcript on disk are
counted and dropped.

## Ground truth

The research session labels by reading; the user is not asked to label.

1. Handover messages, exhaustively: for every sampled session, the
   assistant message in which the task was flipped to unverified or
   unreviewed (locate by the ledger event's timestamp against the
   transcript). Record every command handed to the user in that message
   and how it was written (fence with info string, fence without, inline
   code span, bare prose).
2. Mid-task messages, by random sample: draw assistant messages from the
   same sessions that contain a fence or inline code, outside the handover
   message, and label each code block as command-for-the-user or not
   (error text, file content, TOML, output, example, placeholder).

## Hook events

Read the existing hook log, written by claude-log-hook for every hook
event. For each event kind present, note whether its payload carries
assistant text and whether mid-turn text (between tool calls) appears in
it or only in Stop. No new hook is added; the log already records every
event's payload.

Write a throwaway extractor in the scratchpad that reads the sampled
JSONL, applies a candidate rule (start with: fenced block whose info
string is bash or sh, or an untagged fence whose first line parses as a
shell command), and emits what it would have captured. Score it against
the labels: capture rate on labeled commands, false-positive rate on
labeled non-commands. Try at least one variant of the rule if the first
misses a visible class.

scratchpad; the outcome records its full path so it can be filed as a
tool later if it earns it.

Counts for each of the five context questions, the hook-event table, the
candidate rule with its measured rates, and a one-paragraph recommendation
for E-2531: hook capture, a fence-tag convention, or neither.

payload.context:
## Why

Raised by Mike on 2026-11-01 while planning E-2221 (duplicate marking on
session status boards), from the E-2498 session (ES-1394).

A session that plans a to-be-spawned task has no recorded relationship that
says so. Today a board can only tell that a task has a steward (the session
that keeps it in view until it is spawned or rejected) or that some session
focused it (focus moves on any write). Neither says "this task is being
planned now", and focus doesn't move until the planning session first writes
to the task, so planning is invisible at the start.

Mike: "It would be nice for a session to know another is actively planning it
vs. just being its steward but no planning has started, right?"

## Settled with Mike

- Planning is its own relationship, separate from ownership. It is not
  `task bind`: bind is `task claim` without the worktree and makes the session
  the task's owner. Mike: "when a session plans a to-be-spawned task that is a
  different relationship."
- Focus and stewardship stay separate concerns; this does not tie them
  together. Mike was "cautious about ... unintended consequences of tying them
  together", and sessions routinely write notes and links to other sessions'
  tasks.
- A session marks a task as being planned with `endless task plan start`
  (Mike offered `begin` or `start`; `start` already appears in the CLI,
  `begin` does not).
- `/needs-plan` runs it as its first step.
- Submitting the plan clears it.
- Planning works from any session, including one that has claimed its own
  task: that is where most planning happens.

## Open, for this task's plan

- Whether more than one session may mark the same task at once, and what a
  second `plan start` does.
- How a stale marker clears: the session ends, goes idle, or the user releases
  it, and whether an explicit stop command exists.

# Embed doterr.go instead of importing the go-doterr module

## Code
1. Find the packages that import the module: `git grep -l '"github.com/mikeschinkel/go-doterr"' -- '*.go' | xargs -n1 dirname | sort -u`.
2. In each of those packages, create a `doterr.go` (an empty file with the package's own `package` clause is enough), then run go-doterr's `make sync DIR=<this worktree>` from the go-doterr checkout so every copy is written from go-doterr's `doterr.go`. Never hand-edit a copy.
3. In each package, drop the go-doterr import and the `doterr.` qualifier from every call (`NewErr`, `WithErr`, `StringKV`, and anything else the grep finds). Calling them unqualified is the reason for one copy per package.
4. Remove go-doterr's `require` and `replace` lines from go.mod and run `go mod tidy`.
5. Each copy stamps its errors with its own copy ID, and `WithErr` wraps an error from a different copy in `ErrCrossPackageError`. Check every `WithErr` call: if one enriches an error built by another Endless package, change it so it doesn't (for example, wrap with `NewErr` and pass the error as the cause), and add a test that fails if `ErrCrossPackageError` appears there.
6. `GOWORK=off go build ./...`, `go vet ./...` and the Go tests pass. (Other `replace` lines may still need sibling checkouts; removing those is not this task.)

## Rule
7. Run `endless decision add` once from each of the endless, gomion and go-doterr projects, with the same text: go-doterr is a drop-in, never a module dependency. No go.mod may require or replace github.com/mikeschinkel/go-doterr, except the go-doterr repo's own test/, examples/ and cmd/ modules. A package uses doterr by holding its own copy of doterr.go, synced from go-doterr, so its calls need no package qualifier. go-doterr's doterr.go changes only with the owner's explicit approval.
8. The CLAUDE.md in the go-pkgs parent directory (beside the go-doterr checkout) is in no git repo and outside this worktree, so draft the same rule as a short subsection under "Cross-Package Dependencies" and give the exact text to the owner to paste.

payload.title: Explore running Go fuzz tests as a background job
payload.description: Explore how Endless would run Go fuzz targets as a scheduled background job, feed crashers back as corpus entries or tasks, and bound the run's budget
payload.context:
Fuzz testing has two halves. The search half (`go test -fuzz=...`) is open-ended and pays off by running for hours, so it does not belong in a repo's standard `go test` run. The regression half replays a saved corpus of inputs a past run found and is quick.

Today, in go-cliutil, only the regression half is wired up: `test/corpus_test.go` replays `test/testdata/fuzz/` with a per-entry timeout, and `test/infinite-fuzz.sh` runs the search half by hand, locally, with no schedule and no path for a new crasher to reach the repo. The corpus directory is empty, so the replay proves nothing yet. Other go-pkgs repos have no fuzz setup at all.

Mike raised this while reviewing E-2430 in go-cliutil (2026-11-01): fuzzing is "run it for a long time" work, not "run it fast to catch a regression" work, so Endless should consider running it as a background job rather than in the test suite. The Go-specific pieces may move to Gomion later; for now the whole idea lives in Endless.

Questions to work through:

- Where long fuzz runs live: an Endless background job (the fire-once runner), a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow, or a cron on one of Mike's machines.
- How a run picks its targets: every `Fuzz*` function in a project's modules, or a list the project declares.
- How a run's findings get back: a crasher becomes a corpus entry (committed under `testdata/fuzz/`), a filed bugfix task, or both, and who reviews it.
- Whether the corpus is committed at all, and how its growth is bounded.
- How a run is budgeted: wall-clock per target, per project, per night.
- What Endless owns versus what Gomion will own once the Go-specific parts move there.

payload.title: Decide how to land despite IDE-written changes on main
payload.description: Decide how worktree land can proceed when a JetBrains IDE has rewritten files such as go.mod in the main checkout, without the user quitting the IDE and restoring the files first.
payload.context:
`endless worktree land` refuses to land while the main checkout has
uncommitted user changes. JetBrains IDEs (GoLand, and IntelliJ IDEA with
the Go plugin) keep producing exactly such changes without anyone editing:
whenever go.mod changes on disk, the Go plugin re-syncs modules by running
`go list -m -json all` and then `go mod download -json -x` in the project
root. When the committed go.mod is stale against sibling checkouts named in
`replace` directives, that sync rewrites go.mod and go.sum in place.

Landing E-2520 hit this twice on 2026-11-01. `git restore go.mod go.sum`
cleaned main at 03:22:31; the IDE log shows com.goide.util.GoExecutor
starting `go list -m -json all (endless)` at 03:22:39 and `go mod download
-json -x` at 03:22:40, and the files' mtime is 03:22:40. The land at
03:22:51 failed again with "main has uncommitted user changes". Closing
GoLand did not help because IntelliJ IDEA had the same project open. The
only working path was to quit the IDE, restore, and land back to back.

That workaround is expensive: a JetBrains IDE takes minutes and a lot of
CPU to reopen, and Mike works in one all day. The same sync can fire after
every land that changes go.mod, so the problem recurs with every module
bump. The IDE's write is also a legitimate tidy of a stale file, not a
mistake, which is why plain "the user must clean up" is the wrong framing.

Other IDE-driven writes to the main checkout (.idea/, run configurations,
gofmt-on-save) can trip the same gate, so the brainstorm should consider
the class, not only go.mod.
payload.justification: The IDE's write is correct behavior on a stale file, and the land gate refusing it is also correct; reconciling the two needs options weighed (set aside and reapply, recognize tidy-equivalent diffs, land from a clean clone, IDE settings) before any do-task can be scoped.

payload.title: Support IDEs that work alongside Endless
payload.description: Support IDEs that work alongside Endless by giving them what Endless knows about worktrees and the main checkout, so JetBrains IDEs and VS Code stop indexing, syncing and rewriting what Endless manages.
payload.context:
Endless manages projects whose developers work in an IDE all day, and the
IDE and Endless keep colliding in the main checkout. Two collisions showed
up while landing E-2520 on 2026-11-01:

- JetBrains IDEs (GoLand, IntelliJ IDEA with the Go plugin) index every
  worktree under .endless/worktrees, register each as a VCS root, and run
  a Go module sync (`go list -m -json all`, then `go mod download`) for
  every go.mod they find. With thirty-plus worktrees that is 11 GB and
  570,000 files of indexing and watching, and the IDE log fills with
  "Ignoring change under another root" warnings.
- The same module sync rewrites go.mod and go.sum in the main checkout
  whenever the committed file is stale against sibling checkouts named in
  replace directives, which trips worktree land's clean-tree gate (see
  the related brainstorm about landing despite IDE-written changes).

VS Code has the equivalent surface through gopls, which loads every module
it can see unless told otherwise, plus its own watcher and search settings.

Endless already owns the knowledge the IDE lacks: which directories are
worktrees, when they appear and disappear, and which one a session is
working in. Nothing today passes that knowledge to the IDE, so every
developer discovers the settings by hand, per project, per machine.

This epic collects the IDE-facing work so it is designed once, as a
product feature, rather than fixed one setting at a time. PRODUCT: on
another machine and project the IDE may be any of these or none, its
project files may be absent, gitignored, or committed, and Endless must
never create them or impose an editor on a project that chose none.

payload.title: Exclude worktrees from JetBrains and VS Code project files
payload.description: Exclude .endless/worktrees from JetBrains and VS Code project files when those files already exist, idempotently and without creating them, so the IDE stops indexing, watching and syncing every worktree.
payload.context:
JetBrains IDEs index and watch every directory under the project root
unless it is marked Excluded, and the Go plugin runs a module sync for
every go.mod it finds. With Endless's .endless/worktrees holding one full
checkout per task (11 GB and 570,000 files on 2026-11-01), that costs
minutes of indexing and continuous CPU, registers each worktree as a VCS
root, and runs `go list` and `go mod download` in checkouts the developer
is not working in. Marking .endless/worktrees as Excluded by hand fixes it
for one project on one machine, and nothing remembers to do it for the
next one.

VS Code has the same problem through gopls, which loads every module it
can see unless gopls.directoryFilters excludes the directory, and through
its file watcher and search, which have their own exclude settings.

The exclusion is additive: a JetBrains module's .iml holds excludeFolder
elements inside its content element, and VS Code's .vscode/settings.json
holds files.watcherExclude, search.exclude and gopls directoryFilters.
Both IDEs watch and reload those files, and JetBrains rewrites the .iml on
its own schedule, so an edit must be idempotent and leave every other byte
alone. The IDE project files may be absent, gitignored, or committed.
payload.analysis:
Two reusable packages in the go-pkgs collection would carry the IDE-specific
file handling, so gomion and any other Endless-managed project can share
it:

- go-jetbrains: locate the module .iml (in .idea/ or at the project root,
  depending on the project's age), and add an excludeFolder entry under
  the content element if absent, byte-identical otherwise. Never create
  .idea/ or the .iml.
- go-vscode: read .vscode/settings.json as JSON with comments and trailing
  commas (a strict parser will not do), add entries to files.watcherExclude,
  search.exclude and gopls.directoryFilters ("-.endless/worktrees") if
  absent, preserve formatting elsewhere. Never create .vscode/.

Endless calls both from the project-init path and, ideally, from worktree
creation, since a developer may open an IDE on a project that was
registered before this shipped. Which Endless command owns the call is
open: register, a new `endless ide` verb, or every worktree claim.

Leave .endless/db-ledger alone or make it opt-in: JetBrains already skips
deep indexing of files over about 2.5 MB, and excluding the ledger removes
task history from IDE search for little gain.

A running IDE is the hazard: JetBrains reloads external .iml edits but also
rewrites the file itself. Additive, idempotent edits survive that; a whole-
file rewrite eventually loses a race.

fields.plan:
# Correct anything the ledger tracks

Add `endless correct`, a user-only command that changes tracked state through the ledger and records why. A correction takes two kinds of entry, so that replay and audit each read only what they need.

## Entries

1. `ledger.row_changed` is the change entry. It names the entity type, the row's key and the operation (update, insert or delete), and for an update or insert the values written. It also carries `equivalent_kind`: the existing kind this change resembles (for example `task.status_changed`, `task.fields_updated`, `decision.fields_updated`, `project.updated`, `task.dep_created`, `task.dep_deleted`), left out when none fits. The field is a label only: nothing dispatches on it, so a change entry triggers no existing kind's effects. Executor and projector both apply the entry.
2. `ledger.corrected` is the correction entry. It names the entity, the reason, whether gates were skipped, the before values, and a list of the `ts` values of its change entries. An annotation has an empty list. It writes no database row, and the projector treats it as a declared no-op.
3. One run allocates all timestamps from one clock, appends the change entries and then the correction, and commits them in one ledger commit. The ledger commit subject names the kind and entity, so `git log` shows corrections.

## Command

- `endless correct <entity-type> <id> --set col=value ... --reason <text>` updates a row.
- `endless correct <entity-type> --insert col=value ... --reason <text>` inserts a row. It may set the listed columns plus any column the table requires.
- `endless correct <entity-type> <id> --delete --reason <text>` deletes a row, refusing when other rows refer to it.
- With no `--set`, `--insert` or `--delete`, it records an annotation.
- `--reason` is required. `--skip-gates` bypasses gates and is recorded in the correction entry.
- It refuses when `agent_env.present()` is true.

fields.title: Give every Go task worktree its own go.work
fields.description: Give every Go task worktree its own go.work, written by a Go-support module through a new core worktree extension point at creation and at each spawn, claim or resume, so a main checkout's go.work never breaks it.
fields.plan:
# Give every Go task worktree its own go.work

Go looks for a `go.work` by walking up from the current directory, and a task worktree lives inside its main checkout. A `go.work` in the main checkout is therefore found from the worktree, and Go refuses to build there because the worktree's modules are not listed. A `go.work` in the worktree itself is nearer, so Go uses it instead.

## Core: a generic extension point

1. Add a worktree extension point to Endless's core. It runs after a task worktree is created (in `_bootstrap_task_worktree`, before the project's post-worktree-create hook) and before a session starts in an existing worktree on `task spawn`, `task claim` and `session resume`.
2. The core knows nothing about any language. Extensions register with it, and each decides for itself whether it applies. A failing extension prints an error naming itself and the worktree, and does not stop the spawn, claim or resume.

## Go support: a module outside the core

3. Add a Go-support module that registers with the extension point. It is built into Endless but kept separate from the core, so it can later move to Gomion or call it.
4. It applies to a worktree that has any `go.mod`, ignoring `.endless/`, `vendor/` and `testdata/`. It does not read `projects.language`.
5. If the worktree has no `go.work`, it writes one with `go work init` and `go work use` for every module found, including nested `test/` and `examples/` modules. Go sets the file's `go` line. A worktree that already has a `go.work` is left alone; that covers a tracked one such as go-tealeaves's and the one Endless's own create hook generates.
6. When the file it wrote is not covered by the repo's `.gitignore`, it prints a warning telling the user to add `go.work` and `go.work.sum` to `.gitignore`. It never writes to `.git/info/exclude`.

## Existing worktrees

Worktrees created before this change get their `go.work` the next time a session is spawned, claimed or resumed in them.

## Verification

Tests cover: a new Go worktree under a main checkout with a `go.work` builds; a nested `test/` module is listed; an existing `go.work` is untouched; a non-Go worktree gets nothing; an existing worktree without the file gets it on resume; the warning appears only when `.gitignore` does not cover `go.work`.
fields.analysis:
## Decisions made with Mike while planning

- Write the file at creation and again whenever a session is spawned, claimed or resumed in a worktree lacking one, rather than once for existing worktrees. That also covers a file deleted later, at the cost of one file check per start.
- Write it in every Go worktree, not only when the main checkout has a go.work, so a main go.work added later (by Gomion's go.work command) needs no further step, and Gomion does not have to know Endless's worktree layout.
- Go support is not Endless core functionality. The core gets a generic extension point, and a separate built-in module supplies the Go behavior, so it can later move to Gomion.
- No .git/info/exclude: a hidden entry leaves users unaware that their .gitignore is missing go.work. The module warns instead. Mike's own repos missing the entry get it through their next tasks.

## Costs accepted

A Go worktree runs in workspace mode, so `go mod vendor` refuses there (no repo vendors today), and if a branch raises go.mod's Go version, Go refuses until `go work use` is run; its error names that fix. Endless detects Go by go.mod because projects.language is unreliable: it lists Endless as bash, and many projects have it empty.

payload.title: Show Go's build error when a gotest check fails to build
payload.description: Show the build or setup error a gotest check printed in its -json stream when the verify runner refuses a check that exited non-zero with no test failures, instead of an empty stderr
payload.context:
Found while verifying E-2550 in go-cliutil on 2026-11-06.

A `runner = "gotest"` check composes `go test -json ./...`. Under `-json`,
Go reports a build or setup failure inside the JSON stream on stdout, as
`build-output` actions followed by a package-level `fail`, and writes
nothing to stderr. For example, when a worktree picked up the main
checkout's go.work:

    {"ImportPath":"./...","Action":"build-output","Output":"pattern ./...:
    directory prefix . does not contain modules listed in go.work or their
    selected dependencies\n"}
    {"Action":"output","Package":"./...","Output":"FAIL\t./... [setup failed]\n"}
    {"Action":"fail","Package":"./...","FailedBuild":"./..."}

The runner's gotest-json normalizer counts no test failures from that, so
the run is refused with:

    verify: check exited non-zero but reported no test failures; meta:
    check=0, runner=gotest, exit=1, stderr=

The refusal shows an empty stderr and nothing from stdout, so the one line
that names the cause is invisible. Diagnosing it took reproducing the
command by hand under a stripped environment.

Two ways to surface it, which can both be done:

1. The refusal includes the tail of the check's stdout beside stderr, as
   `tailBytes` already caps stderr.
2. The gotest-json normalizer treats a package-level `fail` carrying
   `FailedBuild`, or any `build-output` action, as a failure of its own,
   reported with the build output as its message, so the run fails as a
   test failure with the cause in the report rather than being refused.

Relevant code: internal/verify/driver.go (runAndNormalize, tailBytes),
internal/verify/gotest.go (the gotest-json normalizer), and wherever the
"exited non-zero but reported no test failures" refusal is raised.

payload.title: Build the task branch without go.work before verify and land
payload.description: Build the branch once with GOWORK=off in the verify and land gates, so a go.mod requirement the per-worktree go.work's replace directives mask fails in the task's worktree before the land, not on main after the fast-forward.
payload.context:
Found while landing E-2357 on 2026-11-07. The land fast-forwarded main, then its build of the installed endless-go failed with "updates to go.mod needed": endless's go.mod required go-dt v0.7.0 while go-cliutil v0.4.0, raised by E-2520, requires go-dt v0.7.1. The drift had sat on main since E-2520 landed, and every verify and land-time build in between passed.

Why nothing caught it: E-2563 writes a go.work into every Go task worktree, with `replace` directives pointing go-dt, go-cliutil and the other house modules at the local sibling checkouts of those modules. Under a go.work with those replaces, `go build` and `go test` never consult the stale requirement in go.mod, so a task's verify passes in its worktree while main, which has no go.work, cannot build. The failure only surfaces after the fast-forward, in the land's own build on main, which is the wrong moment: the merge is already done and the land is half-complete (no migration, no landing record) until someone fixes go.mod on main by hand.

The fix on main was one line, `go mod tidy`, but it had to be made in the main checkout outside any task, and the land of E-2357 then needed a fresh verify because the first land's rebase had moved the branch's SHA.

Shape of a fix: build the branch once with GOWORK=off (or against the module requirements as main will see them) before a verify can pass or a land can fast-forward — in `endless task verify`, in `worktree land --check` (E-2222), or in the land's pre-merge gates — so go.mod drift that the worktree's replaces hide fails the task in its own worktree, where the task can fix it, rather than main after the merge.

The reason is for the person reading the ledger later: the change entry says what moved, the correction entry says why. This holds for every operation, including a soft removal that only sets removed = 1, so that a removal done as a correction is never an unexplained one. Mike settled this while answering EQ-252 on E-2486 and asked that it be persistent rather than re-decided per case.

payload.title: An endless command takes at most one positional argument, scalar or variadic
payload.description: A command declares either one positional argument or one variadic positional argument that takes every remaining value, never two or more distinct positionals. When a command needs several values of different kinds, the extra values are flags, or the command is split into subcommands so that each leaf takes one. Mike set this on 2026-11-01 as an invariant of go-cliutil (ED-1647 in the go-cliutil project), with the reason that multiple positionals make command evolution very difficult: adding, reordering or removing a positional silently changes what every existing caller means, while flags are named and order-free. The rule is the same in every project of his; it is recorded here because Endless has no way yet to record one decision that governs several projects, and the Click CLI in src/endless/ is as bound by it as a go-cliutil command. First applied in Endless to 'endless correct <target> <operation> [KEY]' (E-2486), which had been given two positionals, target and key. See also the Gomion copy.

payload.title: Give sessions a removed flag and live_sessions view
payload.description: Give sessions the removed column, live_sessions view and read-path audit that tasks already have, so a removed session row is retained and its id is never re-minted once a removal path exists.
payload.context:
ED-1547 says no id that anything outside its own row refers to is ever reused.
`tasks` got the treatment in E-1929 (a `removed` column, a `live_tasks` view, an
audited read path); `decisions` gets it in E-2010. `sessions` is the remainder,
and it was deliberately left out of E-2010 rather than forgotten — the reasoning
is below so this task is not re-argued from scratch.

WHY IT WAS DEFERRED, NOT DROPPED

Nothing removes a session today: `git grep "DELETE FROM sessions"` over
internal/ and src/ returns nothing. So this is pre-work — there is no live bug
to fix and no data at risk right now. What it costs is not small: 82 non-test
read sites across 36 files reference `sessions` by FROM or JOIN, and every one
has to be classified as "enumeration, use the view" or "this row specifically,
use the table". Folding that into E-2010 would have buried a live project
data-loss fix (the disk-gone sweep that hard-deleted a project row and cascaded
its tasks and activity away) under the largest read-path audit of the four
entities, for the one entity that cannot yet lose anything.

WHY IT IS STILL REAL

`sessions.id` is declared `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` with no AUTOINCREMENT, which
makes it a rowid alias. SQLite's default allocator is max(rowid)+1, so deleting
the highest session row hands that exact id to the next session created — the
same re-mint hazard the explicit `MAX(id) + 1` allocators carry for tasks and
decisions, just supplied by SQLite instead of by our own SQL. An ES-NNNN id is
written into session_tasks, session_notices, session_statuses, activity, hidden
and pinned task rows, and into task_show output a human reads, so a reused id
silently repoints all of it.

WHAT WILL REACH IT FIRST

E-2486's `endless correct <target> delete` is the first path that can remove a
session. Its plan already reads the right way round — it marks `removed = 1` on
any target whose table has a `removed` column and DELETEs elsewhere — so it is
correct either way and does NOT have to wait for this task. Until this lands,
though, `correct session delete` is a hard delete, mitigated only by its
referrer guard (it refuses when session_tasks, session_notices or hidden/pinned
rows point at the session). A session with no referrers is deletable, and
deleting the highest one re-mints its id.

ORDERING

Preceded by E-2010 for a mechanical reason, not a conceptual one: both tasks add
a goose migration under internal/schema/migrations/, and worked in parallel they
would collide on the same version number. E-2010 also establishes the pattern
(column declared LAST so ALTER TABLE's append position matches schema.sql for
rebuild-db, view body only — never an index, CHECK or generated column naming
`removed`, since those resolve eagerly at CREATE time and would abort a
migration against a DB predating the column).

Deliberately NOT blocking E-2486, and not preceding it either: E-2486 is this
work's only consumer, it degrades correctly without it, and a `precedes` edge
would re-impose the claim refusal that E-2010's land is supposed to clear.

fields.title: Stop hard-deleting projects and decisions
fields.description: Stop the automatic disk-gone sweep from hard-deleting a project row and cascading its tasks and activity away, and give decisions the removed column, live view and shared soft-delete path that tasks already have.
fields.plan:
Two independent halves. They share no files and can be written in either order.

## The project sweep

`endless.project_sync` — the disk-gone branch that currently runs
`DELETE FROM projects WHERE id=?` when a registered project's path is no longer
on disk. Replace it with the retention path the rest of projects already uses:
mark the row `ignored` through the same registry call `endless.unregister`'s
`unregister_project` makes, so the row, its tasks, its activity and its notes
stay and the project revives if the directory comes back. The sweep runs
automatically, so this is the half that is losing data now.

`monitor.ClearIgnoredDirectory` — guards its `DELETE FROM projects` on
`count(*) FROM tasks` being zero, which lets a project with sessions, activity,
notes or deps but no tasks through and cascades all of it away. Widen the count
to every table that references `projects`, or state in the code why tasks alone
are sufficient.

## The decisions half

A goose migration under `internal/schema/migrations/` adding
`decisions.removed INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` and
`CREATE VIEW live_decisions AS SELECT * FROM decisions WHERE removed = 0`,
plus the same two declarations in `schema.sql` — the column last on the table,
the view beside `live_tasks` with the read rule written above it.

One `removeDecision` in `internal/events`, called from
`internal/events/decision.go`'s executor path, its second site, and
`internal/events/projector.go`'s replay path, including the legacy route where a
pre-split `task.deleted` event whose row lives in `decisions` is dispatched.
Parity is the point: a projector that still deleted while the executor marked
`removed = 1` would re-free every removed id on rebuild, on a path nobody tests.

`internal/events/executor.go`'s `SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id), 0) + 1 FROM decisions`
stays pointed at the table. Through the view `MAX(id)` would drop back and the
reuse this change exists to prevent would return while looking fixed.

Then the read audit: every list and lookup of decisions moves to
`live_decisions`; writes, revivals and the allocator stay on `decisions`.
Rows pointing at a decision that never had a foreign key — `task_deps` with
`target_kind = 'decision'` — are left in place and filtered on read through the
join, which is the half of ED-1547 that costs something: the join used to drop
them by accident because the row was gone.

The wipe at `internal/eventcmd/event.go`'s rebuild path is a scoped clear before
replay, not an entity removal, and is left alone.

## Not a resumption of the earlier branch

The branch's single commit is discarded and the work written fresh against main.
It was built when `internal/schema/changes/` was the migration mechanism (now
goose), when projects had no soft-delete design (now status-based, and kept
that way), and when `tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh` was the verification form
(now `.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml`). Eight of the files it edits have moved
or been deleted in main since.
fields.context:
ED-1547: no id that anything outside its own row refers to is ever reused.
Removal sets `removed = 1` rather than DELETE, and every read path then filters
on it.

## The original evidence (2026-08-20)

E-1929 shipped ED-1547 for TASKS ONLY. Its own description said "entities whose
ids something else refers to — tasks, sessions and decisions — are no longer
deleted", but only `tasks` got the column, the view and the read-path audit.
Measured against the real ledger that day: `removed` present on tasks, absent on
sessions, decisions and projects.

195 sessions and 1,616 activity rows vanished when two junk project rows were
unregistered by hand that day. ED-1547 has since been amended to name projects
explicitly and to cover any table added later that meets the same test.

## Revised 2026-11-07, after this task sat unlanded through ~8,600 commits

The task was written when all four entities were open. Three of those four have
since been answered elsewhere, by other tasks, and the remaining scope is
smaller and sharper than the original title.

**Projects: done, by a different design, and kept that design.** E-2251 gave
projects `live_projects AS SELECT * FROM projects WHERE status NOT IN
('ignored','forgotten')`, and E-2349 gave `project forget` a tombstone — name
and path rewritten to `forgotten-<id>`, identity and slug cleared so the UNIQUE
indexes admit a re-registration, the originals kept as JSON in `forgotten_from`.
`unregister` and `purge` no longer destroy anything.

Measured against the "act like it never existed" test, that design's two statuses
split: `forgotten` IS `removed = 1` and could be replaced by it with nothing
lost, but `ignored` is NOT. An ignored row is a positive assertion — "this is
not a project, do not auto-register it" — and the directory-to-project resolver
has to FIND it, because being found is exactly what stops auto-registration.
Unifying on `removed = 1` would restore the auto-registration E-2251 exists to
prevent. Projects are also machine-specific rather than project-specific and are
headed for their own database, which is the better place to settle it. So
projects are left alone here.

**One project hard delete survives, and it is automatic.** The disk-gone sweep
in `endless.project_sync` still runs `DELETE FROM projects`, while `tasks` and
`activity` still carry ON DELETE CASCADE from `projects` — the exact mechanism
that cost the 195 sessions, now firing without anyone typing a command.
`monitor.ClearIgnoredDirectory` deletes too, guarded only on the project having
no tasks, so a project with sessions and activity but no tasks is deleted and
cascades them. These are the live bugs and they are the reason the task stays
open.

**Decisions: not done, and the semantics are settled.** Three hard deletes
remain, there is no column and no view, and the explicit `MAX(id) + 1`
allocator still re-mints. `removed` is the right mechanism rather than a status
value: `removed = 1` means "act like this decision never existed", while
proposed, accepted, rejected, supersedes and reconsidered are all workflow.
Settled by the user on review, against the open work to evolve decisions into
decide-tasks, which is orthogonal.

The hazard is real but has not fired: there is no command that removes a
decision, the ledger holds 7 `decision.deleted` events and all 7 target the same
id (dev churn during one task), and that id is an interior hole — only the top
of the range is ever re-freed — so `max_id = 1652, n = 245` and no decision id
has ever actually been reused. Which is why this half is cheap rather than
urgent, and why no removal CLI is added with it.

**Sessions: not done, nothing to convert, deliberately deferred.** Nothing
removes a session today, so there is no live bug; the cost is 82 non-test read
sites across 36 files. Filed as its own task rather than folded in here, so the
project data loss above is not held behind the largest audit of the four for the
one entity that cannot yet lose anything.

**The earlier branch is discarded, not resumed.** It was written against
`internal/schema/changes/` (replaced by goose in E-2019), before the projects
design existed, and with a `tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh` gate (replaced by
`.endless/tasks/<id>/verify.toml`). Eight of the files it edits have moved or
been deleted in main.

payload.title: Rename task.deleted to task.removed
payload.description: Rename the task.deleted event kind to task.removed and retire the old spelling so replay still accepts it, making the event name match both the command that emits it and the row retention it performs.
payload.context:
ED-1547 reserves two words, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than
stylistic. A covered entity — one whose id something outside its own row refers
to — is **removed**: the row stays, `removed = 1` is set, the id is never
re-minted. A pure row handle, a surrogate primary key nobody stores or types, is
**deleted**: the row is gone and its id is free. Reading `removed` in the ledger
should tell you the id survived; reading `deleted` should tell you nothing did.

`tasks` is a covered entity and has been soft-removed since E-1929. The command
says so — `endless task remove`. The event it emits says the opposite:
`task.deleted`. So the one durable record of what happened describes a hard
delete that did not occur, on the entity whose id retention ED-1547 exists to
guarantee.

## The mechanism is already in the codebase

`events.RetiredKinds` (internal/events/event.go) exists for exactly this, and
its comment says so: "a retired one that only replay will ever see". It holds
four kinds today. The change is to add `task.removed` to `ValidKinds`, move
`task.deleted` to `RetiredKinds`, and have the executor and projector dispatch
both spellings into the one removal function. No history is rewritten — the
ledger keeps both spellings forever, and only the new one is ever emitted again.

## Secondary, and cosmetic

`session_tasks.removed` is the same contradiction running the other way: a
junction row with a surrogate id, genuinely hard-deleted, named "removed". By
ED-1547's own words — "deleting a junction-table row is unrestricted" — it
should be `session_tasks.deleted`. It is the same two maps in the same file, so
it is nearly free to do here, but it is cosmetic: no id guarantee rides on it
and no reader is misled about data that survived. Drop it if it is not worth the
churn.

## Why it is not folded into E-2010

E-2010 renames `decision.deleted` to `decision.removed`, because it is already
rewriting that handler and adding that column, and shipping new retention
behavior under a name that says "deleted" would bake the contradiction in
deeper. The task rename is different: it is a pure rename of shipped, working
behavior that touches nothing else E-2010 touches, and a ledger-compatibility
change deserves review on its own rather than riding inside a data-loss fix.

Conflicts with E-2010 rather than following it: both edit `ValidKinds` and
`RetiredKinds` in the same file, so they must not be in flight together, but
neither needs to come first.

fields.title: Check go.mod tidiness without go.work in every verify
fields.description: Check every Go module in a task worktree with go mod tidy -diff under GOWORK=off as the first row of endless task verify, re-rooting relative replace paths to the main checkout, so an untidy go.mod fails in the worktree, not main after the land.
fields.plan:
One new built-in check in `endless task verify`, written in Go beside the runner, plus its documentation.

**The check.** A new package, `internal/gomodcheck`, holds the pure parts and one runner: `Modules(worktree)` finds every go.mod under the worktree outside `.endless/`, `vendor/`, `testdata/` and `.git/`, the rule `go_support.go_modules` uses; `RerootModfile(src, mainModuleDir, dst)` copies a go.mod rewriting each replace path that begins with `./` or `../` to the absolute path it resolves to from `mainModuleDir`, and copies the go.sum beside it; `Run(moduleDir, mainModuleDir)` writes the copy into a temporary directory, runs `go mod tidy -diff -modfile=<copy>/go.mod` with GOWORK=off and `moduleDir` as the working directory, and returns pass, or the diff and go's stderr on exit 1, or an error for any other failure. `mainModuleDir` is the module's path relative to the worktree root, joined to the main checkout root (the parent of `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`). The check is skipped as a whole when the main checkout root contains a go.work.

**Wiring in the runner.** `internal/verifycmd` runs the check before the suite's own checks, once per module found, and reports each as a check row named for the module (`go.mod is tidy without go.work` for the root, with the module's relative directory appended for a nested one). The row carries the diff and the remedy, `go mod tidy` in that directory followed by a commit, when it fails, and it is fail-fast like the suite's first native test. With no Go module in the worktree nothing is added, so non-Go projects see no change. The `go` on PATH is the one used; a `go` older than 1.23 fails the row naming the version.

**Tests.** `internal/gomodcheck` tests with the real `go` tool: a module whose go.mod understates a transitive requirement fails with a diff naming the version; a tidy module passes; a module with a relative replace that resolves only from the main checkout's location passes after re-rooting; a replace for a module not in the require list is tolerated; nested modules are each found and the excluded directories are not. A `verifycmd` test shows the row first in the report for a Go worktree, absent for a non-Go one, and absent when the main checkout has a go.work.

**Docs.** `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` gains a short section under "Writing one" saying that every Go worktree's run begins with this built-in row, what it checks, and the remedy; the "per-task verification suite" topic in `docs/guide/orchestration.md` gets one sentence pointing there.

**Endless itself.** On landing, the first Go task to verify meets the row; its go.mod is tidy as of E-2357's land fix, so it passes unless something drifts again.
fields.context:
Found while landing E-2357 on 2026-11-07. The land fast-forwarded main, then its build of the installed endless-go failed with "updates to go.mod needed": endless's go.mod required go-dt v0.7.0 while the local go-cliutil checkout it is replaced with, raised by E-2520, requires go-dt v0.7.1. The drift had sat on main since E-2520 landed, and every verify and every pre-merge build in between passed. The fix was one line of `go mod tidy`, but it had to be made in the main checkout outside any task, and E-2357 then needed a fresh verify because the failed land's rebase had moved the branch.

Why nothing caught it: Go's workspace mode. When a go.work is in effect, `go build`, `go vet` and `go list -m all` all accept a go.mod that understates a requirement; with GOWORK=off the same commands refuse with "updates to go.mod needed". Proven on a toy module during planning. E-2563 writes a go.work into every Go task worktree, so every verify runs in workspace mode while the main checkout, which has no go.work, does not. Endless's own worktrees also carry replace directives in that go.work, written by the project's post-worktree-create hook through `just go-work-init`, but they are not the mask: a go.work holding only `use .` masks the same way.

PRODUCT: a user's plain Go project gets the same go.work from E-2563 on day one, and the land builds nothing on main outside self-dev, so for them the drift surfaces nowhere at all. Their main checkout simply stops building, with no message from Endless.

One more fact shapes the fix: endless's go.mod replaces its go-pkgs modules with paths relative to the main checkout's parent directory. From a task worktree, three directories deeper, those paths do not exist, so a plain `go mod tidy -diff` in the worktree fails with "replacement directory does not exist" before it can say anything about drift.
fields.analysis:
## Decisions made with Mike while planning (2026-11-07)

**The check is `go mod tidy -diff`, not a build.** Mike's call: being stricter than main's build is a good thing. An untidy go.mod is the very thing that broke the land, so the check holds go.mod and go.sum tidy, not merely buildable. The one-time cost is that the first Go task to verify after this lands fails until someone runs `go mod tidy` and commits it; that task can fold the tidy in. `go mod tidy -diff` needs Go 1.23 or later, exits 1 when go.mod or go.sum would change, and prints the change as a unified diff. It operates on the single module and ignores go.work, so the check sets GOWORK=off for certainty and documents that it is belt and braces.

**Relative replace paths are re-rooted, not worked around.** Mike's proposal: rewrite each relative replace path so it resolves where main's go.mod would resolve it, and check the result is a real directory. Go's `-modfile` flag makes this clean: the check writes a copy of go.mod into a temporary directory, rewrites every `=> ./x` or `=> ../x` replace path to the absolute path it would have from the module's counterpart directory in the main checkout, copies go.sum beside it (tidy reads the go.sum next to the modfile), and runs `go mod tidy -diff -modfile=<copy>` with the module directory as the working directory. Verified from the E-2357 worktree against the stale go.mod: exit 1 with exactly the one-line go-dt diff; against the fixed go.mod: exit 0. A replace for a module that is not in the require list is left to Go, which tolerates it, so endless's own `go-gitutil` replace, whose path is written for a worktree's depth and does not resolve from main, does not fail the check.

**The gate lives in the verify runner.** A built-in first check in every Go worktree's run, so the agent meets it on its own verify, before the handoff, and the user sees it in the report and the CTRF like any other check. The land needs the user's passing verify at the branch's current commit, so it is protected through the same row. With a module-graph check rather than a compile, the cost on a docs-only task is small.

**Skipped when the main checkout has its own go.work.** Some repos (go-cliutil and go-cfgstore among them) keep a go.work in the main checkout. There main builds in workspace mode too, so nothing is masked relative to it, and a strict check would refuse a go.mod that main accepts. Mike accepted this without fully weighing it and will revisit if it bites.

## Decided without asking

- A Go module is detected as E-2563's writer detects it: a go.mod outside `.endless/`, `vendor/`, `testdata/` and `.git/`. `projects.language` is not consulted. The rule is duplicated in Go because the runner is Go and the writer is Python; it is four names.
- One check row per module found, root and nested, since main builds each on its own.
- The failure is a check row, first in the report and fail-fast, not a refusal before the suite, so it lands where the user reads.
- A `go` older than 1.23 fails the check naming the version needed rather than skipping, because skipping would reinstate the mask silently.

## Rejected alternatives

- `GOWORK=off go build ./...`: main's exact verdict, but no stricter than it, and a compile per run. Rejected for the tidy check at Mike's direction.
- A temporary checkout of the branch beside the main checkout, at its depth: reproduces main exactly, including relative replaces, but costs a checkout and a build per run and leaves a directory beside the user's repositories if a run dies. The -modfile rewrite gets the same resolution for free.
- Dropping the relative replace directives from endless's go.mod: would make the plain check work here, but changes the go-pkgs workflow (main would build against published versions), and is repo work, not product work.
- Wiring the check into the land gate or `worktree land --check` (E-2222): later than the agent's own verify, and E-2222 is underway in another session. The land is already protected by needing a verify at the current commit.
- A line in a project-level `.endless/verify.toml`: no core code, but off by default, so a product user gets the mask from the go.work Endless wrote and nothing to warn them.

They run only after an UPDATE matched nothing, and their whole job is to tell "no such row" from "wrong status" — which the retained row answers and the view does not.

Consistency with the tasks implementation is the reason; the cost is that a future `decision remove` command would want the guards added, which is why the departure is stated here rather than left in the diff.

entries.note: runGoModChecks runs before setup and the suite's checks in both runner paths (manifest and legacy verify.sh); each module's row is a one-test report that fails the run through the merged summary. The row is first in position; the suite's other checks still run, as a failing first native test does.

gomodcheck.Modules walks the worktree pruning .endless, .git, testdata and vendor (go_support.PRUNED_DIRS mirrored); one row per module, the root's with the bare label and a nested module's with its directory appended.

RerootModfile rewrites ./ and ../ replace paths, one-line and block forms, to filepath.Clean(mainModuleDir/path) — cleaning is load-bearing: Go treats a/../b and b as different directories and reports ambiguous imports otherwise. go.sum is copied beside the copy; tidy runs with -modfile and GOWORK=off in the module directory. The main checkout is the parent of git rev-parse --git-common-dir; a directory outside git is its own main checkout.

The failing row's message carries the diff, tidy's stderr when any, and 'Fix: run `go mod tidy` in <dir>, then commit go.mod and go.sum'. When replace paths were re-rooted it adds that they resolve from the main checkout's location, since a plain tidy in the worktree stops at them (true of this repository).
Skipped as a whole when <main checkout>/go.work exists; Modules returning none adds nothing. Both covered by runner tests.
`go env GOVERSION` is read first; below go1.23 the row fails with its own message naming the version found and go1.23, and tidy is not attempted. Tested with a fake go on PATH.

All five cases run the real go tool on fixtures with directory replaces (GOPROXY=off), plus MainCheckout against a real git worktree and the old-go case through a fake go; runner tests cover row order, the failing row, the non-Go worktree, the go.work skip and the old go.
